<explanation>
Based on the provided file tree and README, the project is a Java SDK built for the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Essentially, it is a modularized library that enables Java applications to interact with AI models through both synchronous and asynchronous communication mechanisms. It also offers Spring Boot integration via separate modules (WebFlux and WebMVC) that act as client and server starters.

Below is a step-by-step guide for drawing an accurate system design / architecture diagram tailored to this project:

1. Identify the Main Components:
   • MCP Core Library (located in the “mcp” directory): This is where the essential protocol definitions, clients, servers, transport implementations (HTTP SSE, Stdio, etc.), and utility classes reside.
   • MCP BOM (“mcp-bom” directory): Acts as the Bill of Materials to ensure dependency versions and module coordination across the SDK.
   • MCP Spring Integration (“mcp-spring” directory): Contains two distinct modules:
     – mcp-spring-webflux: Provides non-blocking, reactive connectors (using WebFlux) for both client and server components.
     – mcp-spring-webmvc: Provides traditional Spring MVC-based integration, especially for server side provisions.
   • Test Components (“mcp-test” directory and tests in other modules): Include a comprehensive suite of tests covering client and server interactions, integration tests, and transport validation.

2. Determine Relationships and Interactions:
   • Show how applications (or external systems) use the MCP Core Library as the central piece to initiate communication with AI models.
   • Indicate that the Spring integration modules wrap around or extend the core’s functionalities, offering pre-configured starters for those using Spring Boot.
   • Represent that the BOM acts as the glue between multiple modules, ensuring consistent dependency management.
   • Clearly display the testing components interacting with the main libraries to validate both synchronous (McpSync…) and asynchronous (McpAsync…) functionalities and various transport mechanisms.

3. Highlight Architectural Patterns and Design Principles:
   • Modularity: The separation of concerns is evident—core protocol definitions are separated from Spring specific integrations and test suites.
   • Extensibility: The use of interfaces and provider patterns (as visible in the transport packages) implies that the SDK is designed for extensibility.
   • Separation of client/server and synchronous/asynchronous capabilities. Diagram labels should clearly denote these distinctions.
   • In the Spring integration modules, differentiate between reactive (WebFlux) and servlet-based (WebMVC) approaches.

4. Include Relevant Technologies, Frameworks, or Libraries:
   • Java SDK (core language and libraries).
   • Spring Boot, separating WebFlux and WebMVC for reactive vs. traditional server environments.
   • Maven (as evidenced by the pom.xml files, wrapper scripts, and Maven Central related workflows).
   • CI/CD integration (GitHub workflows indicate automated builds and releases).
   • SSE (Server-Sent Events) implementations for client/server transport.

5. Guidelines for Tailoring the Diagram:
   • For this type of SDK, focus on defining the core module first along with its key interfaces (client, server, and transport providers), then branch out into how the Spring modules provide integration points.
   • Emphasize how the modules interact (e.g., core module provides the base, while Spring modules “wrap” this into the Boot context).
   • Clearly differentiate between modules that are used in production (mcp, mcp-spring) and testing utilities (mcp-test, embedded tests across other modules).

6. Diagram Elements to Include:
   • Clear labels and boxes for each component:
       - A large container for “MCP Java SDK”.
       - Sub-containers for “MCP Core”, “MCP BOM”, “MCP Spring WebFlux”, “MCP Spring WebMVC”, and “MCP Test”.
   • Directional arrows:
       - Arrows pointing from external applications to the MCP Core (client/server interactions).
       - Arrows showing how the Spring modules integrate with the core library.
       - Arrows indicating dependency management flowing from the BOM to each module.
   • Use color codes or distinct shapes to differentiate between modules that provide core functionality, integration, and testing.
   • Optionally, illustrate protocol flows (for both synchronous and asynchronous operations) within the core module, highlighting transport strategies (e.g., HTTP SSE, Stdio).

7. Final Assembly:
   • Start with a high-level box labeled “MCP Java SDK” which branches into the main components outlined above.
   • Use sub-divisions for the Spring modules to detail client/server flows.
   • Annotate flows with interaction patterns (e.g., “Async Client → Core Protocol → Async Server”).
   • Include notes for configuration management (via Maven/BOM) and testing that ensures the correctness of these interactions.

When drawing the diagram, be as detailed as possible—label every module and key interface, use directional arrows to indicate the flow of data or dependencies, and adopt a consistent color or shape scheme to differentiate between distinct types of system components. This approach will provide a clear, comprehensive, and accurate representation of the SDK’s overall architecture geared towards integration and extensibility within modern Java and Spring-based applications.
</explanation>
